string.text: {=spc_wc2_0_prebackstory}My story? I am glad to tell it, if it interests you.

{=spc_wc2_0_backstory_a}My father learned siegecraft in the days of Sultan Alp Arslan. In those years our horsemen could break any army in the field, yet the humblest Byzantine fortress could still shame us - we knew nothing of rams or mines or siege towers.

{=spc_wc2_0_backstory_b}So the Sultan offered gold, weight for weight, for any Byzantine engineer taken alive. Those captives were made to teach men like my father the art of breaking walls. My father, in turn, taught me.

{=spc_wc2_0_backstory_c}In the old days, an apprentice who left his master's service for another lord could expect a very unpleasant death if caught. But times change. The richest cities have already fallen, and what walls remain are built higher than before. The beys pay less for a siege-master now, and pay it late. So I have come looking for other work, if any is offered.
{=spc_wc2_0_backstory_d}In any case - if you find some inconvenient wall standing between you and what you desire, and wish to see it reduced to rubble, you know where to find me.
{=spc_wc2_0_response_1}Of course. A good engineer earns every dinar of his pay.
{=spc_wc2_0_response_2}How loyalty has decayed since the old days.

{=spc_wc2_0_generic_backstory}My father was one of the men Sultan Alp Arslan had trained by captured Byzantine engineers. Our people knew little of siegecraft before that. He was bound to serve the Sultan alone, on pain of death, but he taught me his trade, and these days I am free to serve whoever pays.
{=spc_wc2_1_prebackstory}You would think a hall like this could pour a decent kumis instead of this excuse for wine... but never mind. You asked for my story.

{=spc_wc2_1_backstory_a}I rode for years under my bey, before he was even a bey. I had a good name and a fair purse. There was a girl in a neighboring encampment - quiet, but strong hips for bearing sons - and I thought she would make a fine wife.

{=spc_wc2_1_backstory_b}So I went to her brother and offered fifty sheep, a generous bride-price. He said he would not give his sister to 'a man like me.' I asked what he meant. He gave no answer, so I struck him. Perhaps twice, no more. It shouldn't have killed a real man, but the whelp died on me.

{=spc_wc2_1_backstory_c}You know how it goes after that - his kin came to our camp looking for my blood. They didn't find me, but they wounded one of my cousins. It was time to answer them, but my brothers lost their nerve and struck a bargain instead. I was made to leave. What do you make of that?
{=spc_wc2_1_backstory_d}I'll tell you what I make of it - I am sick of cowards, sick of men who won't stand by their own blood.
{=spc_wc2_1_response_1}True enough. Honor is as rare as a hen's tooth these days.
{=spc_wc2_1_response_2}Strange, how few men wish to die for someone else's quarrel.

{=spc_wc2_1_generic_backstory}I rode under my bey's banner for years and should have had a place of honor at his fire. Instead I killed a man from a richer family over an insult, and he had too many kinsmen for me to stay.
{=spc_wc2_2_prebackstory}I come from one of the frontier Turkmen clans, far to the east. I do not know if you understand our ways - I will try to explain.

{=spc_wc2_2_backstory_a}A man of another clan killed my father. My father had killed his uncle, years before that. It fell to me to avenge him, but plague took the killer first - so I was expected to kill his brother instead. That is how it is among us.

{=spc_wc2_2_backstory_b}I wanted to go to the other clan and settle the matter with words instead of blood. I had always had a gift for ending quarrels, and it seemed to me that fate itself had already closed the feud. But my mother begged me not to go. My cousins begged me not to. They said I should spill blood, not talk.

{=spc_wc2_2_backstory_c}My family said the other clan would mock my father's memory, that no one would fear us anymore - that our flocks and our women would be taken. They told me: do your duty, or you are no longer of our blood. So be it. I chose exile. Why should more men die for a debt that death has already paid?

{=spc_wc2_2_backstory_d}If an enemy stands before me in a battle line, I will loose my arrows at him without hesitation. But this - killing a man for a crime that was never his - I could not accept it. I left my people. Here, at least, I choose what I do.
{=spc_wc2_2_response_1}A noble choice.
{=spc_wc2_2_response_2}What - does no one honor their family's name anymore?

{=spc_wc2_2_generic_backstory}My clan was bound to another in a blood feud for years, life for life, generation after generation. I chose to break the chain and left my family rather than kill a man who had done me no wrong. It happens among us, from time to time, though few speak of it.
{=spc_wc2_3_prebackstory}Very well - I'll tell you a soldier's tale, if you have the patience for it.
{=spc_wc2_3_backstory_a}I've fought under three different beys now. But I fight on foot - my family is town-born, not steppe-born. Life is different for men like us.

{=spc_wc2_3_backstory_b}The horse-lords, the tribal riders - they gallop here, gallop there, loosing arrows left and right. They win battles, I won't deny it. But when the fighting is done and the enemy is still laughing behind his walls, all that galloping counts for nothing.

{=spc_wc2_3_backstory_c}We foot-soldiers are the ones who climb the ladders into the meat-grinder. I did that for fifteen years, for less pay than some boy fresh off his mother's knee who happens to own a horse. I'd had enough, so I went looking for other work.
{=spc_wc2_3_backstory_d}Whatever the case, I'll fight for any man willing to share the risks his soldiers face.
{=spc_wc2_3_response_1}Well said. Good infantry is the spine of any army.
{=spc_wc2_3_response_2}Resentment poisons an army. A soldier follows the orders he's given.

{=spc_wc2_3_generic_backstory}I was a spearman, and I fought on foot - that's what you do if your family has no horses of its own. Twice the danger, half the pay, none of the glory. I've had my fill of it, and I'm looking for other work now.
{=spc_wc2_4_prebackstory}I'll tell you my story. If you mean to judge me for it, you're welcome to, but I've no wish to hear it.

{=spc_wc2_4_backstory_a}My clan was among the last Turkmen still living the old way, moving from pasture to pasture. Not a large clan - you would not have heard its name. It grew smaller still when a Byzantine patrol fell on our camp and scattered our flocks. Those of us who survived took shelter with a larger clan, one whose name I will not give you.

{=spc_wc2_4_backstory_b}They protected us, but they treated us with contempt - fetch this wood, carry that water. We bore it, for the sake of our elders and our nursing mothers. But it sat poorly with the young men.

{=spc_wc2_4_backstory_c}Perhaps I was prouder than most, or quicker to anger. One of them insulted my lineage, and I answered in kind, poorly chosen words that I have long regretted. Our protectors said they would shelter us no longer while I remained. So my own clan cast me out.

{=spc_wc2_4_backstory_d}A man must eat. It's easy enough to take a trader's horses on the road - but unless he wishes to live like a beast, a man also needs someone to buy what he takes, and give him bread and a blanket in return. There are merchants in these towns who ask few questions, and sometimes have other work besides.
{=spc_wc2_4_response_1}Misfortune is no reason to accept humiliation.
{=spc_wc2_4_response_2}As they should have. A man who curses his protectors deserves no home.

{=spc_wc2_4_generic_backstory}My clan lost its herds and land to a Byzantine raid, so we swore ourselves to a stronger clan's protection. They treated us as servants. I finally stood up for myself and killed one of our so-called protectors in the fight that followed. They call that a great shame - but it seems to me that once you've tasted defeat, shame finds you no matter what you do.
{=spc_wc2_5_prebackstory}Ah... very well, I can satisfy your curiosity.

{=spc_wc2_5_backstory_a}Some boys learn to plant crops with their fathers. Some learn to herd sheep. I spent my childhood learning to work the alleys outside the wine-houses. My father taught me. A cruel man, but a good teacher.

{=spc_wc2_5_backstory_b}If a man was drunk enough, I could lift his purse and he'd never know it - though sometimes a light knock on the skull was needed. Travelers only, mind you - much less trouble afterward. Every trade wants finesse, my father used to say.

{=spc_wc2_5_backstory_c}A wise man, my father. But proud, and pride was his undoing. A thief cannot afford pride. We don't last long without the guards looking away, and a new captain wanted to double what my father paid him. He refused. They hanged him for it.
{=spc_wc2_5_backstory_d}I am proud too, so thieving is closed to me now. I am looking for work that doesn't require me to bow to the whims of guards and gaolers.
{=spc_wc2_5_response_1}There's something to be learned from a man skilled at any trade, I suppose.
{=spc_wc2_5_response_2}Sounds like justice, to me.

{=spc_wc2_5_generic_backstory}My father was a thief and, when he had to be, a killer - we preyed on drunks and travelers outside the caravanserais. The guards caught up with him eventually. He had enough silver saved to buy freedom for one of us. He chose me. He was hanged, and I ran.
{=spc_wc2_6_prebackstory}I will tell you, though if you favor the Sultan's house, you may not care for it.

{=spc_wc2_6_backstory_a}You know the Turkmen once lived free upon the open steppe. But our beys grew fond of comfort - palaces, trade, the wars of kings. Three decades past, the Sultan decreed that every clan must settle and hold fixed land, so their warriors could be counted and levied, their flocks counted and taxed. Most obeyed - they had come to prize comfort over freedom.

{=spc_wc2_6_backstory_b}Some resisted. You may have heard of them, still out on the grass, raided for slaves by their own kin now, cast out as outlaws. My people were broken up in smaller measure - some bands were lured in with silver, others hunted down and beaten, their sons taken as hostages.

{=spc_wc2_6_backstory_c}Mine was one of the clans hunted down a generation ago for refusing the decree. They took our flocks. We have lived like beggars on the edge of the towns ever since. The far grass calls to us still, but a man without sheep cannot go there and live.

{=spc_wc2_6_backstory_d}I have scraped together some coin - I won't say how - enough to buy a sword. I mean to earn what was taken from my people: herds of our own again. I know little of the steppe now, I'll admit, but I know the back streets, the shadows, how to grow strong where I stand.
{=spc_wc2_6_response_1}Such a cruel decree.
{=spc_wc2_6_response_2}A wise decree. Nomads are the enemy of good order.

{=spc_wc2_6_generic_backstory}A generation ago the decree came that every clan must settle, to be counted and taxed. My people refused. Their men took our flocks, and we have lived on the edge of the towns ever since. I mean to earn the coin to buy new herds, and go back out into the grass, beyond any lord's reach.
{=spc_wc2_7_prebackstory}Oh yes. I do have a story worth telling.

{=spc_wc2_7_backstory_a}Raiders took me when I was a girl. There are old tales of warrior-women out on the far steppe, and my buyer decided I would make those tales real - to fight other captives, for the amusement of his guests.

{=spc_wc2_7_backstory_b}Perhaps there is something to those old tales after all, because I did very well for him, and made him a wealthy man in the process. The law forbids killing in the public arena now, but no one asks what happens behind closed doors at a rich man's table - and more than a score of my fellow captives have felt my blade.
{=spc_wc2_7_backstory_c}I feel no guilt for it. They were trying to kill me, and some came close enough. I did what was needed.

{=spc_wc2_7_backstory_d}There's little else to tell. My master was a cruel animal, but he let me keep my winnings, and in time I bought my freedom - perhaps he also saw where it would end, had he kept me against my will. So here I am, making my living the only way I know how. Have you work for me?
{=spc_wc2_7_response_1}I suppose you did what you had to.
{=spc_wc2_7_response_2}Necessity or not, you seem to take some pride in it.

{=spc_wc2_7_generic_backstory}I was taken captive as a girl and sold in the city, to a man who had me fight other captives for his own amusement. In time I bought my freedom, and now I intend to enjoy it.
{=spc_wc2_8_prebackstory}If you wish to know how cruel one's own people can be, I could enlighten you.

{=spc_wc2_8_backstory_a}My father died shortly after my mother learned she was carrying me. I was her only child, and like most of our women, she had wanted a son. So she raised me as one, and boasted of me the way she would have boasted of a son - how swiftly I nursed, how well I brought down steppe birds with my bow, and later, that I would be the first of my age to bring home an enemy's head.

{=spc_wc2_8_backstory_b}Because I loved her, and because I was quicker and stronger than the boys, I did everything she promised I would. I was the first of my year to kill in battle. She boasted louder still, until the other women came to hate her for it. They drove us both from the camp. We had to sell our land and our servants for a fraction of their worth, since we could not carry them with us - all we kept were our sheep. Raiders found us soon enough. They killed my mother and took the flock. I got away.

{=spc_wc2_8_backstory_c}I wandered the grass a while, and went hungry more than once. But I followed the raiders, and when one of them wandered past the firelight to relieve himself, he did not return. I kept his purse. And his sword.
{=spc_wc2_8_backstory_d}I could go back to my people, I suppose. I have no wish to. So here I am, in the towns, earning good coin with my sword and caring nothing for who envies me.
{=spc_wc2_8_response_1}I'm sorry for your loss. Life dealt you a cruel hand.
{=spc_wc2_8_response_2}Every day I thank the heavens I was not born to savages.

{=spc_wc2_8_generic_backstory}My father died before I was born, and my mother raised me as the son she never had. When our clan turned on us out of envy, raiders finished what jealousy started - they killed my mother and took our flock. I took one of their swords and a horse, and rode away.
{=spc_wc2_9_prebackstory}You can't sell a horse without shouting its praises, as they say.

{=spc_wc2_9_backstory_a}I was the brat of a caravan guard. Never knew my mother, but my father kept me close. I grew up running between the camels' legs on the trade road, listening to merchant gossip in the caravanserais, fed sesame cakes by the other guards. You couldn't ask for a happier childhood.

{=spc_wc2_9_backstory_b}But once I was older, it wasn't so simple to bring me along - too many young men giving me strange looks. My father wanted a good husband found for me, but the boys he knew weren't the marrying sort in his eyes. So I told him: I'll be like you, Father - I'll carry a blade and guard rich men's goods. Perhaps some decent man will love me for my earnings, if not for my family's name. He grumbled, but he had no better plan.

{=spc_wc2_9_backstory_c}So here I am. I've little interest in the marriage part, if I'm honest, but I do like the coin, and I like my freedom. Perhaps one day I'll surprise him with a fine plot of land to see him comfortable in his old age.
{=spc_wc2_9_backstory_d}As I said: I can ride, I can use a blade, I can run a caravan, and I have a fair head for turning a profit. Do you know anyone in need of that?
{=spc_wc2_9_response_1}I'm sure he'll be glad, so long as you are.
{=spc_wc2_9_response_2}You must have broken your poor father's heart.

{=spc_wc2_9_generic_backstory}I was a caravan guard's daughter, raised on the trade road, and I decided long ago I'd rather be the one guarding the goods than the one preyed upon by bandits. I have the skills for it now.
{=spc_wc2_10_prebackstory}Mm. Go on, then, ask.

{=spc_wc2_10_backstory_a}I grew up in a village not far from here. My father was a peddler, and I went with him from door to door, buying broken things, mending them, earning a coin here, a coin there. You know how the horse-lords look down on those of us who scrape and save for the tax collector - trampling our crops, dragging our sons off to war, sitting up in the saddle looking pleased with themselves while we grub in the mud.

{=spc_wc2_10_backstory_b}In any case, that life wasn't for me. So I made up my mind to run off to the free clans that answer to no sultan and take in strays. Karluk, they're called, out past the frontier. Only trouble was, I needed a horse first.

{=spc_wc2_10_backstory_c}So I hung about the marketplace, looking for a likely one. Found a fine animal whose owner hadn't tied it properly before wandering off to drink. I took it and ran. And wouldn't you know it - the wretched beast threw me before I was a mile out of town, and trotted straight back to its sodden master.

{=spc_wc2_10_backstory_d}In any case, I need a new plan for making my way in the world. I won't be a peddler like my father, that much I've decided. Perhaps I'll learn to fight and ride, or perhaps I'll run caravans of my own one day - one way or another, I mean to find my place among the hawks of this world, not the pigeons.
{=spc_wc2_10_response_1}Well - I suppose you've got spirit.
{=spc_wc2_10_response_2}Ha! May every thief fail as badly as you did.

{=spc_wc2_10_generic_backstory}I was a village peddler's son, and that's not the life I want. I mean to learn to fight and ride. There are plenty of lads like me in these parts, whatever the horse-lords think of us.
